item.title: Human-Centered Learning Mechanics: Observable Entropy Control under Protected-Risk Constraints
item.description: arXiv:2605.22940v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Human-Centered Learning Mechanics (HCLM) treats learning as an open, controlled process in which task progress, representation information, structural restrictions and externally specified risk limits jointly govern parameter updates. We characterise this mechanism through a normalised covariance-information force, metric observability and exact feasible rate constraints. The projected task rate depends on an observable cross-product that differs from the ordinary task information product when a probe set does not contain the training task. Error, finite-step and delay margins specify when admissible local requests can be implemented. A primary 288-run neural study separates information control from empirical risk protection and retains cases where extra compression worsens held-out loss. Follow-up experiments train the observable restriction in a declared 13-dimensional subspace, implement a frozen-public-encoder readout through an actual Gaussian sample channel, evaluate a fixed-coefficient sensitivity grid, and test targeted nuisance control with two-hidden-layer minibatch learning on Fashion-MNIST. The nuisance study improves shifted accuracy over ERM, while generic protected balancing accounts for most of the gain. Together, the theory and experiments identify attainable information actions, predictive costs and the separate assumptions required for population-risk certification.
item.dc:creator: Kim Phuc Tran

item.title: Can Tabular In-Context Learners Generalize to Biomolecular Property Prediction?
item.description: arXiv:2606.31126v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Predicting biomolecular properties from limited labeled data is a central bottleneck in protein engineering and small-molecule design. As strong pretrained encoders now supply rich fixed-length representations, the difficulty has shifted from representation learning to building a data-efficient predictor for the few-shot regime. Tabular foundation models such as TabPFN and TabICL perform this prediction through in-context inference after pretraining on synthetic tables. We test whether they can act as flexible interpolators over informative fixed biomolecular representations. Treating each method as a predictor-representation pair, we evaluate across two domains. On ProteinGym, TabPFN3-ESMC600M is competitive with leading supervised-substitution entries and obtains the lowest MSE among the leaderboard-context rows considered, while Kermut remains stronger by Spearman. Performance is substantially lower under modulo and contiguous holdouts than under random splits. On the five-endpoint PpEST dataset, tabular models show favorable descriptive performance against matched supervised baselines, but the random split measures within-family interpolation and the small endpoint count precludes strong model-ordering claims. For small-molecule classification with ECFP/RDKit descriptors, no single predictor-representation pairing dominates across TDC ADMET, MoleculeNet, FS-Mol, and DrugOOD, but several pairings are competitive with strong descriptor and graph baselines. Crucially, on both protein and small-molecule few-shot tasks, these predictor-representation pairs offer strong performance. We conclude that tabular foundation models can be strong biomolecular predictors, but only when coupled with expressive representations.

item.title: Improved Quantum Algorithms for Reinforcement Learning Under a Generative Model
item.description: arXiv:2608.02826v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Reinforcement learning is a subfield of machine learning that studies how an agent interacts with an environment in order to extract as large a reward as possible. A standard approach to study such interaction is through Markov Decision Processes (MDPs) and the task of choosing an optimal policy---a function that tells the agent which action to take. In this work, we study two types of time-dependent MDP---finite-horizon and infinite-horizon discounted---and propose new quantum algorithms for computing approximate optimal policies. Our quantum algorithms are based on a new combination of standard value iteration and quantum subroutines like quantum mean estimation and quantum maximum finding, overall enhanced with techniques from sample-optimal classical algorithms. Our resulting query complexities improve upon previous works, thus approaching already established quantum lower bounds.
item.dc:creator: Joao F. Doriguello

item.title: Online Non-Monotone DR-Submodular Maximization Beyond $1/e$ with Feasible Gradient Queries
item.description: arXiv:2609.02145v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We study adversarial online maximization of nonnegative, non-monotone DR-submodular functions over compact convex down-closed sets $K\subseteq[0,1]^d$ when gradients may be queried only at feasible points. The online approximation coefficients $4/9$ (Aggarwal and Lu) and $2\sqrt{3}-3\approx 0.4641$ (Aggarwal and Du) rely on queries along chains that start from the all-ones vector and leave $K$. With every query in $K$, the best known coefficient was $1/e$. We give an online algorithm with coefficient $0.4013$ that, in each round, plays a random action, queries one gradient at a point of $K$, and makes one projection. Its expected approximate regret is $O(RB(1+R)\sqrt{T})$, where $R\le\sqrt{d}$ bounds the norm of points of $K$ and $B$ bounds the gradient norm on $K$. For a budget $\sum_i x_i\le k$, the bound is $O(kB\sqrt{T})$. The algorithm keeps a state $x\in K$, and the analysis applies the coordinate-chain comparison of Aggarwal and Lu inside the box $[0,x]$, which keeps every query feasible. A second comparison, along a path from $0$ in the direction $x$, cancels the extra terms that the box creates. Because the queries are feasible, they can be played, which gives regret $O(T^{2/3})$ under semi-bandit feedback and $O(T^{4/5})$ under bandit feedback with bounded values. Unbiased stochastic gradients with bounded second moment keep the $\sqrt{T}$ rate, and on a fixed function the algorithm attains $0.4013\,\mathrm{OPT}-\varepsilon$ in expectation with $O(1+R^2(1+R)^2B^2/\varepsilon^2)$ feasible gradient queries.

item.title: Compatible Likelihoods for Flow Matching on Manifolds
item.description: arXiv:2610.31981v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: On the simplest non-Euclidean manifold, the 1D flat torus, we exhibit a distribution where a recent extension of Riemannian flow matching is globally optimized by a velocity field that pushes samples away from the data distribution. We trace this failure mode to a property we call compatibility; a likelihood-based flow matching objective is compatible if its population minimizer recovers the marginal velocity field induced by the data and coupling. We derive a general condition for compatibility, apply it to existing methods, and bound the worst-case error by a residual term that vanishes under compatibility. On compact manifolds, we show that existing compatible objectives put density on infeasible velocities. To tackle both issues, we propose an exponential family over endpoints with the conditional velocity as sufficient statistic, which is both compatible and supported only on feasible velocities. In practice, and with low overhead, this reduces to a reweighting of the flow matching loss. On spaces of constant curvature, this treats errors in flow speed and direction differently. Compared to prior art, our method finds the correct velocities on the test case, outperforms in general on high-dimensional product tori, and, for two of four standard geospatial benchmarks on the sphere, achieves substantial NLL improvements. When evaluated on a large dataset of human poses, our method surpasses prior work according to sample-based metrics.
item.dc:creator: Lucas Ng, Georgios Batzolis, Mark Girolami

item.title: Out-of-the-Box Tabular Foundation Models for Bayesian Optimization in Materials Discovery
item.description: arXiv:2611.12491v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Bayesian optimization is widely used in active learning loops for materials science. Gaussian processes serve as the de-facto surrogate model family, but require task-dependent kernel choices and can lack the modeling capacity for complex relationships. Tabular foundation models (TFMs) have recently emerged as the state-of-the-art for predictive tasks on structured data, without requiring bespoke kernels or hyperparameter tuning. We evaluate two TFMs, TabPFN and TabICL, as out-of-the-box surrogate models on two standard materials science benchmarks, comparing against a large field of baselines encompassing Gaussian processes, random forests, and CatBoost. Our findings indicate that TFMs are highly competitive surrogate models across the two benchmarks, without task-specific training for active learning or GP kernel selection. Our results motivate developing TFMs further as surrogates for active learning in materials discovery.
item.dc:creator: Klemens Fl\"oge, Simon Bing, Leo Grinsztajn, Eliott Kalfon, Lennart Purucker, Noah Hollmann, Frank Hutter
